title: Developer Who Cloned Photoshop With AI Now Builds Word, Excel and PowerPoint Replicas
excerpt: Brandon Thomas's WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft are free, open-source Rust replicas built with Claude - impressive in scope, but still alpha software at roughly half to three-fifths real-work readiness.
body:
• Developer Brandon Thomas, who built free open-source replicas of Adobe's Creative Cloud apps with Claude, has now released WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft - replicas of Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.
  • The three apps are written in Rust with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, released under MIT or Apache 2.0 licences, and read and write real .docx, .xlsx and .pptx files.
  • They are early alpha software: TechSpot reports roughly 60% feature parity for WordCraft overall, GridCraft about 50% ready for real work and DeckCraft about 55%.
  • For readers: the apps are free to try on Windows, macOS and Linux, but the reported parity figures mean they are not yet a safe replacement for Office on critical work files.

The developer who used AI to clone Photoshop has now taken on Microsoft Office. After building free, open-source alternatives to Adobe's Creative Cloud apps using Claude, developer Brandon Thomas has released replicas of Word, Excel and PowerPoint, according to TechSpot. The new apps are called WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft.

All three are written in Rust with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, as the Adobe replicas were, and are available under MIT or Apache 2.0 licences. TechSpot stresses they are still at a relatively early stage and need more work before they can be considered viable alternatives to Microsoft Office. That caveat matters: the surface can now be rebuilt quickly with AI help, but depth is a different test.

What each app does

WordCraft is described on its GitHub page as an open-source, clean-room reimplementation of Microsoft Word. It runs natively on Windows, macOS, Linux and BSD, can be used in a browser via WebAssembly, and uses a single Rust codebase without Electron or Tauri. It reads and writes .docx, supports .odt, .rtf, .html, .md and .txt, imports the legacy .doc format, and exports PDFs with selectable text, links and bookmarks. Spelling, grammar and many other features work offline, Thomas noted. Visually it offers Word's ribbon, styles, tables, track changes and references, and it implements mail merge from a CSV file or Outlook contacts.

GridCraft, the Excel replica, already implements 89% of Excel's ribbon and menu commands and about 98% of its worksheet functions, according to the developer figures reported by TechSpot. It uses .xlsx as its native format, offers the formula bar and keyboard shortcuts, and is fully scriptable by AI agents. DeckCraft opens and saves .pptx files, aims for full PowerPoint parity, and claims 79% feature parity across 191 PowerPoint features, including advanced formatting and PDF export.

WordCraft is the furthest along, with 88% of Word's ribbon commands implemented but only around 60% overall feature parity. GridCraft is around 50% ready for real work and DeckCraft around 55%, TechSpot reported. Those gaps are instructive: recreating menus is fast, while formatting and compatibility are where Office has decades of accumulation.

From Adobe clones to Office

The Office replicas follow Thomas's seven Adobe-style apps under the ArtCraft name, including PhotoCraft, the Photoshop replica. Its PhotoCraft GitHub repository describes a clean-room reimplementation of Photoshop rebuilt in pure Rust, with layers, masks, adjustment layers and real PSD files, and the project's site is at ArtCraft. Other coverage, including Thurrott's report on the Office launch, put WordCraft at 87% of ribbon commands and about 62% real feature parity, GridCraft at 93% of worksheet functions in that account, and DeckCraft at about 79% of PowerPoint's feature set - broadly in line with TechSpot's figures, with small differences between reports and project pages as the code moves.

The projects have been dismissed by some as AI slop. The verifiable point is narrower: these are real, downloadable programs that open real Office files, built by a very small operation with a frontier model doing much of the coding labour. Whether they become durable alternatives depends on file fidelity, not launch-week attention.

What it means for Office users

For Indian and diaspora professionals who live in Word, Excel and PowerPoint for work, the immediate value is optionality, not migration. A free, offline, cross-platform app that opens a .docx or .xlsx without a Microsoft 365 subscription is useful for a second machine, a Linux laptop, or quick viewing and light edits. The reported parity figures - roughly half to three-fifths ready for real work - are a clear warning not to trust these alphas yet with a client deck, a financial model with complex functions, or a document whose formatting must survive a round trip exactly.

The longer question is for Microsoft and Adobe. If replicas can reach this stage in weeks with AI help, subscription software's moat shifts to collaboration, cloud integration and perfect compatibility - none of which Thomas's apps offer. What they show is that the floor of what one developer can rebuild has risen sharply.
